section.title: Graph sketching with calculus
section.p: The first derivative tells where a graph rises and falls. The second derivative tells where it bends upward and downward.
A graph sketch is not a guess. It is a summary of evidence.

subsection.title: Asymptotes and end behavior
subsection.p: Polynomials do not have vertical asymptotes. Rational functions often do.
Derivative information describes shape where the function exists. Limits describe what happens near missing points and far away.

subsection.title: A complete curve-sketching workflow
subsection.p: A calculus sketch should gather evidence in an organized way.

li.p: Find asymptotes and end behavior with limits.
Compute f'(x) and make a sign chart.
Use f' to find increasing/decreasing intervals and local extrema.
Compute f''(x) and make a sign chart.
Use f'' to find concavity and inflection points.
Plot reliable points and sketch a graph that obeys all the evidence.

subsection.p: The workflow is not a rigid machine. Sometimes symmetry saves work. Sometimes a limit matters more than a derivative. Sometimes a derivative is too complicated to factor nicely. But the questions are steady.

subsection.p: The sketch is not only a picture of the formula. It is a picture of the evidence.

subsection.title: When technology helps and when it misleads
subsection.p: A graphing calculator or computer can help check a sketch, but it should not replace the analysis.
Technology draws what it samples. It can miss a hole, hide an asymptote, or make a bad viewing window look convincing.

A graphing device may draw the line y=x+1 without showing the missing point at (1,2). But the original function is not defined at x=1. The correct graph is a line with a hole.

note.p: Algebra and domain information can reveal what a plotted graph hides.

paragraphs.title: A misleading window
paragraphs.p: The function
has vertical asymptotes at x=-1 and x=1. But if we only graph it on the window
we see only the middle branch. The graph may look like a small decreasing curve with a flat point at the origin. That window hides the asymptotes and the outer branches.

subsection.p: A graphing device answers the question we ask it. Calculus helps us ask better questions:
Where is the domain broken?
What happens near the broken points?
What happens as x\to\pm\infty?
What do f' and f'' say?
A good sketch uses both tools: computation for speed, and calculus for judgment.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: Graph sketching often leads back to limits. A vertical asymptote is a limit. A horizontal or slant asymptote is a limit. End behavior is a limit.
Some limits are easy. Others have a strange form. For example,
